props.title: Burnt Money

sections.content: Burnt Money (2000) ignited a new wave of Latin American crime cinema with its raw portrayal of doomed romance and criminal desperation. Director Marcelo Piñeyro crafts a searing true-crime story based on the notorious 1965 heist gone wrong in Argentina. The film follows gay lovers Angel and Nene as they attempt a dangerous bank robbery, channeling the intense criminal passion of Bonnie and Clyde (1967) while adding complex layers of sexuality and class warfare. Like Dog Day Afternoon (1975), it transforms a heist narrative into a character study of desperate outsiders.

sections.content: The film's visual style draws from both classic noir and the kinetic energy of Latin American New Cinema. Director Piñeyro uses handheld cameras and natural lighting reminiscent of City of God (2002), creating an immediate, documentary-like feel that heightens the tension. The relationship between Angel and Nene echoes the tragic criminal couples in Breathless (1960) and They Live By Night (1948), but with an explicitly queer perspective that was groundbreaking for Latin American cinema at the time.

The film's exploration of criminality and sexuality influenced later works like Bad Education (2004) and The Skin I Live In (2011). Its unflinching portrayal of violence and desire challenged both mainstream and queer cinema conventions, paving the way for films like Weekend (2011) and Moonlight (2016) that refuse to sanitize or sensationalize LGBTQ+ stories. sections.content: Burnt Money marked a crucial shift in how Latin American cinema depicted both crime and queer relationships. Unlike earlier films that coded homosexuality through suggestion, like Law of Desire (1987), Piñeyro's film presents its characters' sexuality matter-of-factly while focusing on the universal themes of loyalty, betrayal, and the destructive nature of obsession. This influenced later works like The Way He Looks (2014) and Plan B (2009).
